## Report: Does Add-On Cannabidiol Reduce Convulsive Seizure Frequency in Children with Dravet Syndrome?

**Conclusion:** The evidence does **not** support the view that this claim is false. On the contrary, multiple randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, a systematic review/meta-analysis, and long-term open-label extension data consistently show that adjunctive cannabidiol (CBD) reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome.

### Key Evidence

1. **Landmark RCT (Devinsky et al., 2017, NEJM):** A multinational, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of 120 children and young adults (ages 2–18) with Dravet syndrome found that CBD (20 mg/kg/day) produced a significantly greater reduction in convulsive-seizure frequency than placebo over14 weeks (median reduction ~39% vs. ~13%). Adverse events were more common with CBD. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618))

2. **Dose-ranging RCT:** A double-blind trial randomizing 199 children to CBD (10 or 20 mg/kg/day) or placebo showed convulsive seizure frequency reductions of ~48.7% (10 mg/kg/day) and ~49.7% (20 mg/kg/day) versus baseline, both superior to placebo. ([Springer/PMC review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10949818/))

3. **Systematic review & meta-analysis (2020):** Pooled data from three large placebo-controlled trials confirmed a greater reduction in convulsive seizure frequency with adjunctive CBD versus placebo. ([Springer meta-analysis](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6))

4. **Long-term open-label extension:** Sustained reductions in convulsive and total seizure frequency were maintained up to 48 weeks, with acceptable safety. ([Wiley/Epilepsia](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628))

### Important Caveats

- **Clobazam interaction:** Some researchers have questioned whether CBD's benefit is partly mediated through interaction with clobazam (a common co-medication), raising the level of N-desmethylclobazam. This is a legitimate confound but does not negate the overall clinical finding. ([ILAE](https://www.ilae.org/journals/epigraph/epigraph-vol-22-issue-3-special-journal-prizes-issue/cannabidiol-and-clobazam-elucidating-interactions-to-improve-epilepsy-treatment))
- **Adverse events:** CBD was associated with higher rates of adverse events (somnolence, diarrhea, elevated liver enzymes), and more trial withdrawals occurred in the CBD group.
- **Industry funding:** The pivotal trials were funded by GW Pharmaceuticals (maker of Epidiolex), which is worth noting for potential bias.

### Bottom Line

The claim is **well-supported** by high-quality randomized controlled trial evidence, meta-analytic confirmation, and long-term extension data. The view that it is false is not consistent with the published evidence. The main legitimate criticisms concern the magnitude of benefit, the role of clobazam interactions, adverse-event burden, and industry funding—not the existence of a treatment effect.
